questions.prompt: What can $I30 index slack recover that the $MFT and USN journal cannot?
options: The full content of deleted files
Filenames and $FN timestamps of deleted files even after their MFT records have been reused and overwritten
The user who deleted the file
questions.explanation: Deleted index entries frequently remain in the unused space of allocated index pages, naming files that no longer exist anywhere else on the volume.

questions.prompt: How does $LogFile differ from the USN journal in coverage and detail?
options: $LogFile holds full redo/undo transaction detail over a much shorter window; the USN journal holds a summary per change over a longer one
$LogFile covers a longer window than the USN journal
questions.explanation: $LogFile is the highest-resolution filesystem artifact and the most perishable, often covering only hours on a busy volume.

questions.prompt: Why does $LogFile rank near the top of the order of volatility for disk-side evidence?
options: It is stored in RAM rather than on disk
Its window is measured in hours on a busy volume, so it wraps far faster than other filesystem artifacts
It is deleted at every shutdown
It requires a live system to read
questions.explanation: Heavy write volume means the transaction log recycles quickly, making early collection essential if it is to be useful at all.

questions.prompt: An attacker created, filled, archived, and deleted a staging directory. Nothing is in the MFT, the USN journal wrapped, and carving found nothing. What may still identify the files?
options: $I30 index slack, which may still list the filenames with their original $FN timestamps
questions.explanation: Index slack will not recover content, but proving a specifically-named file existed in a specific directory is frequently the entire question.
